cim: Why Artificial Intelligence May Never Be Truly Conscious, No Matter How Smart It Gets
cim_eredeti: Why Artificial Intelligence May Never Be Truly Conscious, No Matter How Smart It Gets
szoveg_eredeti:
A chatbot may be able to reason, remember, and change its mind. But it has nothing at stake, because it has no body to lose.

A philosophical position called functionalism says that consciousness is about what something does, not what it’s made of. So, if AI gets to the point where it can hold a conversation, reason, remember, change its mind, exhibit curiosity and emotions, and so forth, then it doesn’t matter if it’s made of flesh, silicon, or LEGO bricks. In fact, some have suggested that denying consciousness to such a creature would be a new type of small-minded bias.

I am willing to go out on a limb and say that, despite what leaders at some AI companies have suggested, I know the LLMs I talk with aren’t conscious … not for empirical reasons, but because I don’t think the concept makes sense.

My line of thought begins with a famous thought experiment called the Chinese Room, posed by the philosopher John Searle (1932–2025), who, in 1980, asked us to imagine finding ourselves in a room with a slot and no other openings. In the room are careful instructions in English for correlating “scribbles” with other seeming scribbles, using a gigantic book of such correlations. Then a note in Chinese is slipped into the room. We don’t speak Chinese or even recognize Chinese characters as a language, but we look up the marks, write the marks the book tells us to, and slip the results back through the slot.

The correlations let Chinese speakers outside the room be certain that they’re having a meaningful conversation with someone who understands Chinese. But all we’re doing is manipulating odd marks on paper that are utterly meaningless to us.

Searle maintains that this is exactly what computers do, including ones that seem conscious: They’re manipulating symbols without any awareness of what the symbols mean, or even that they’re symbols at all. The Chinese Room shows us that symbol manipulation is not enough to constitute consciousness because the meaning of a symbol comes from a consciousness separate and apart from it. In Searle’s terms, that makes the meaning of a symbol extrinsic to it: it has to be applied by a consciousness apart from the symbol.

Consciousness like ours, on the other hand, is different. When you burn your hand on a hot pot handle, take a bite of a banana, or put your left foot in front of your right as you stroll, you don’t need to translate those into pain, the taste of bananas, or walking. Your brain is part of a living body that directly feels pain, tastes food, and knows how to walk without looking down. No symbols required, no translations needed. In Searle’s terms, that means consciousness is intrinsic: it doesn’t need another consciousness to assign meaning to it.

But where does the intrinsic nature of consciousness come from? Searle doesn’t tell us.

Ahalf-century before Searle, Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) already had. In his 1927 masterpiece, “Being and Time,” he looks at the world not as we explain it, but as we experience it in ordinary, everyday circumstances. He found that, with surprising regularity, our understanding is out of sync with our experience.

Instead, he noted, in everyday lived experience, things almost always show themselves to us in light of our current project or intentions: For example, if you don’t have a glass for drinking, the empty jam jar may look like a cup. With a different project, it might show itself as a possible temporary flowerpot. We thus experience the world in two lights simultaneously: our project and the thing’s possibilities with regard to that project. Both of those show us the world in terms of what matters to us at that time and in that circumstance.

Heidegger says it’s because we know we’re at risk. But that still wouldn’t explain anything unless we care about being at risk. And that puts us in a loop: We care because we know our projects and our own lives are always at risk. But care is why that risk matters to us. Around and around we go.

Heidegger brings this loop down to our knowledge that we are going to die someday — maybe even today. And we care about that. But again, why? Although Heidegger doesn’t talk about it directly, I think we can extend his thinking to say it comes down to our being embodied. The loop stops there because caring is intrinsic to bodies — the sort of stopping point Searle was looking for. Care needs to be intrinsic to us because bodies need to avoid pain, to eat and sleep, and to be guided carefully by pleasures. Sleepiness, hunger, pain, and pleasure are intrinsic in that they are not symbols that need interpretation, not to mention that your body is also intrinsically you, and you are intrinsically your body.

Care and embodiment are deeply entangled.

When a slice of apple cake tastes good, its pleasant taste is not an act of interpretation. Neither is the pain you feel when you stub your toe. And when your child crawls into your lap to be cuddled, you may take it as a sign of love, but that’s because your body already felt that love; at no point was it like an ink mark in a language you don’t understand. Our bodies are our first and primary source of intrinsic experience. And that experience is shaped by the many ways we can care about things.

Now, care might sound like the ultimate generalization about human consciousness — as in “It all comes down to care.” Yet care is always specific in at least three ways in our everyday experience.

First, care always has an object it cares about and a specific way it cares about it. That might be a partner or child, but it could equally well be the socks in the dryer, that itchy spot on your back, or your goldfish that needs feeding.

Second, the context of care is always specific as well: You care about your socks because it’s cold out, your itch because it’s calling out to be scratched, your goldfish because your kids will be sad if they find it floating upside down (not to mention, you’ve grown attached to it yourself).

Third, care is also sensitive to details. A moment of acute caring about another person can be a response to the way they are looking at you, a gesture that embodies a feeling you can’t quite place, or the way they are leaning forward as they listen closely. Caring often finds truth in the particulars.

The specificity of care is shaped by the world into which we were born. To emphasize the bruteness of this fact, Heidegger calls it thrownness: Without our consent, each of us is born into a culture, a language, a place, a family, and so on. This is what it means to be situated — which is what happens to beings that, as embodied, cannot simultaneously be in multiple places or times.

Thrownness shapes our bodies as well as our minds. The philosopher and feminist Iris Marion Young (1949–2006) brilliantly explores this in her 1980 essay “Throwing Like a Girl.” She offers a descriptive analysis of how the typical situation of a girl raised in a place like America affects even her most casual bodily actions — how girls carry books or walk on stones across a stream — and imposes an “I cannot” on many of the projects they contemplate.

This can only happen because experientially we’re not stuck inside a room receiving cryptic symbols that we need to interpret. We embodied beings are out in the world where the wetness of our bodies in a sudden storm is not a symbol. Our embodiment is this intrinsic, direct openness to the world. That is exactly what AI lacks.

David Weinberger is a best-selling author, Harvard researcher, and former philosophy professor. He is the author of “Beautiful Particulars,” from which this excerpt is adapted.
